utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we call the next witness, Mr. Krajisnik, it's, I would say, a shared experience of all human beings how it feels after you've seen the dentist. I hope that you're not feeling too bad, that you're still comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very grateful for the Trial Chamber having given me the possibility of seeing a dentist. I don't feel bad. And once again, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It goes without saying, dental care is one of the things the Detention Unit should provide to the extent needed. Then, Mr. Gaynor, the next witness is a 92 bis witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct. The next witness is Osman Selak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Who will be testifying without protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Without protective measures. And I did understand that you wanted to submit also some of the exhibits that were presented during his testimony in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Your Honours have expressly asked to be provided with one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And we've selected six others which we consider to be the most -- of greatest value to Your Honours in reviewing his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What's the way in which you -- you just --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yeah. I've discussed it with the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What I suggest we do is first of all we tender a CD containing the transcripts themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And then I would tender the exhibits -- I will read the number from the Brdjanin case into the record to assist in cross-reference. I'll then tender all of the exhibits with a separate number in this case. And I don't propose to ask the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The witness any questions at all about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. The video, which is on your list, is a lengthy video which was not in its entirety played in Brdjanin, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if we are going to admit it, it would be more than was tendered and admitted in Brdjanin. I take it, at least, that only those portions that were played were admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't know whether they admitted the entire video or simply those portions in the Brdjanin case. What I can do, if you prefer, is select -- regardless of what was admitted in the Brdjanin case, select the portions of that video which are of most relevance to this case, and I can select the transcript portions and submit those and dispense with the CD version of the video, whichever Your Honours find most useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, would you have any views on the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm wondering whether the simplest course wouldn't be simply to -- well, what was admitted in Brdjanin presumably is accompanied by a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's played in court. And from what I remember, is that we have the transcript -- at least, the text is reproduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, it seems to be sufficient for -- for this trial's purposes that the -- the text is on the transcript, unless the Prosecution consider that the actual video is of some extra materiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, another way of dealing with it would be to -- to limit the admission of those portions of the -- of the videotape that are reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's of course not the same thing. It's still the video. But limited portions of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, Your Honour, after all it's -- perhaps some of the experience in this case is that the -- there's many instances in which the actual video doesn't really add anything to the text is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't seen it, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I was saying, Your Honour, unless the Prosecution is suggesting that this is a case where it really does add something, we can simplify things by just dispensing with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'd prefer to review the transcript and the video and make the selections. The most critical participants are actually on pages 1 and 2 of the transcript. There may be other parts which are of utility to Your Honours. And if we could defer a decision on, this I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then hear from you at a later stage. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile we could ask Madam Registrar to assign exhibit numbers to the exhibits listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, would you be in a position to give the Brdjanin exhibit number for the video to Madam Registrar so that she can better work on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The video to be reviewed is P1594 in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Selak. Do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is handed out to you now by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Selak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, you have been called as a witness. The Prosecution has submitted to the Chamber your testimony in the Brdjanin case, and that's admitted into evidence. Just for the public, Mr. Gaynor will briefly summarise the content of that testimony, and the reason that you are called is to give an opportunity to the Defence to cross-examine you on -- on these issues. Mr. Gaynor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly. Examined by Mr. Gaynor:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you confirm your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Osman Selak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, as the Judge has just indicated, I'll read into the record a summary of the evidence which you gave in the Brdjanin trial and I'll read slowly. Colonel Osman Selak is a Bosnian Muslim. He was a professional soldier in the JNA from 1955 until 1992. By 1992, he was a colonel and in charge of logistics for the Banja Luka area of command. Upon the creation of the VRS, he applied for retirement. Pending his application, he served from 18th May to 10th July 1992 as one of the few Muslim officers in the VRS. The witness did not personally attend any meetings of the VRS Main Staff, nor any meetings with any members of the Republika Srpska Presidency. The witness previously gave testimony in the Brdjanin trial about the transformation of JNA units in Bosnia and Herzegovina into the VRS. The witness also testified about the command structures in the JNA and the VRS. He testified about reporting structures within the VRS, including the requirement for twice-daily reports from commanders to the VRS Main Staff and the requirement for troops on the ground to report every principal stage of task implementation to their superiors. Colonel Selak described the ethnic composition of the JNA and the VRS and instances of discrimination and propaganda directed against Muslim and Croat soldiers and officers. He testified about the dismissal of Muslim and Croat officers and the confiscation by the VRS of their property after they had fled from their homes. He also testified about the relationship between the Serb Territorial Defence forces and the JNA. Contrary to JNA regulations, Colonel Selak was ordered by General Uzelac to provide weapons to Serb Territorial Defence units that were not mobilised. He also testified about the distribution at night of weapons to Serb civilians at their homes. Colonel Selak also testified about military operations of the Banja Luka Corps conducted against Muslim and Croat civilians. He testified about VRS military operations against non-Serbs in Kozarac in May 1992. The witness testified about a meeting at which both he and General Talic were present. VRS operations at Kozarac, including the killings and arrests of civilians, was discussed at the meeting. Colonel Selak also testified about the creation of the Manjaca prison camp. The witness testified about regular contact between the VRS and political organs in Banja Luka and about cooperation between Serb military and political leaderships to achieve their joint objective. He also testified that information was provided by municipality presidents to VRS units to assist those units in carrying out their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I propose to just address one subject with this witness. Prior to doing that, I'd like to tender, as we discussed earlier, a number of exhibits from the Brdjanin case. And I will read out the Prosecution's exhibit number in this case as well as the Brdjanin case while I do this. The first exhibit, which was P1588 in the Brdjanin case, is a combat report dated the 1st of June, 1992 to the Main Staff of the Army of the SR BH from Lieutenant Colonel Stanimir Djurovic; that is P734 in this case. The next exhibit is a document authorised by Colonel Mico Grubor, which is transmitting an order of the Main Staff of the VRS. This document is dated 21st of June, 1992. It was Exhibit P1584 in the Brdjanin case. It is Exhibit P735 in the Krajisnik case. The next exhibit is an order to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps from Colonel General Ratko Mladic dated the 9th of June, 1992. It was Exhibit P1583 in the Brdjanin case. It is Exhibit P736 in the Krajisnik case. The next exhibit is a short videotape of a speech by Colonel Pero Colic on the 2nd of August, 1992. The Brdjanin exhibit number was P1596. In the Krajisnik case, the exhibit number for the video version of the speech is P737, and the transcript is P737A. The next exhibit is a report dated the 27th of May, 1992 to the Republika Srpska BH army Main Staff. It's a report on the elimination of the Green Berets. This was Exhibit P1587 in Brdjanin and P738 in the Krajisnik case. The next exhibit is dated the 9th of June, 1992. This was sent to the SR BH army Main Staff and the SR BH Presidency. It was sent from Colonel Milutin Vukelic. This exhibit was Exhibit P1582 in the Brdjanin case and it's Exhibit P739 in this case. That's the exhibit which Your Honours expressly requested to be provided with. The final exhibit which I will deal with at a later date was P1594 in the Brdjanin case, and I'm instructed will be P740 in this case. And the transcript will be P740A. Now, I'd request, Your Honours, to concentrate on the last of those exhibits, which is the exhibit which Your Honours expressly requested. And I'd like the witness to be shown a copy of that exhibit, please. That's P739.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Selak, you might recall having a look at this in the Brdjanin case. As you can see, it was dated the 9th of June, 1992. It's a report submitted to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina army Main Staff and the SR BH Presidency. And it says in the first paragraph: "One of the issues that was discussed at yesterday's session of the AR Bosnian Krajina Crisis Staff was the general personnel policy in the army 1st Krajina Corps." It goes on to say: "It was stated that within the units of the 1st Krajina Corps, 14th PoB, and the units of the RV i PVO in Banja Luka garrison there are 67 officers of Muslim or Croat nationality." Stopping right there, could you tell us what the 14th PoB was.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: That's the 14th logistics base of which I was the commander. It provided all the units in Bosanska Krajina with logistics, the 1st Krajina Corps and the other units that were in that area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you just clarify how many men you were commander of.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: After THE mobilisation had been carried out in May 1991 and in September 1991, there were about 2.300 or 2.500 men, give or take a few hundred men, but that was roughly speaking the figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, this document goes on to say: "An ultimatum was issued" -- this is the middle of the first substantive paragraph: "An ultimatum was issued requesting removal of these persons from vital and command posts by the 15th of June, 1992 or they will take over the control of the armed forces. We consider this demand to be justified." At the end of the paragraph, it says: "The 1st Krajina Corps Command should make the decision as to which staff members from the ranks of Muslims and Croats may be temporarily -- may still be temporarily kept and at what posts." Now, Colonel Selak, I'm going to direct your attention to a question you were asked about this paragraph in the Brdjanin case and the answer that you gave. The prosecuting lawyer asked you whether you were surprised that this document went to the Main Command of the army but also to, as it were, the head of state. This for cross-reference purposes is on page 13068 of the Brdjanin transcript of the 17th of January, 2003. To that question, as to whether you were surprised, you said: "No, that does not surprise me." You were then asked: "So that's something you would have expected in respect of this kind of issue." You replied: "The question here is very important. It pertains to the survival, to the life of the people in an area. And according to my opinion, this information is something that is expected. It's not something that surprised me."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's this type of information, I think, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "This type of information is something that is expected. It's not something that surprised me. Members of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina regularly visited the corps command and toured the units of the front." Now, I just want you to focus on the last sentence which you gave in your response, and I'll just repeat it: "Members of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina regularly visited the corps command and toured the units at the front." Now, I want you to explain whether you personally saw any members of the Presidency visit the corps command and tour the units at the front.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was never personally present. I never saw them in the corps command or in the units. But the media, the newspapers, et cetera, would regularly --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... he's answered the question then. He was asked whether he'd personally seen them, and he has. Your Honour, this witness, 92 bis application, and then there's a supplement in this area, but the witness has now answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next question would be: If you did not personally see it, what information you had available which make you testify that members of the Presidency regularly visited the corps command and toured the units at the front. Could you tell us what -- on the basis of what information you gave this testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the president of the Serbian Republic, Karadzic, arrived on one occasion to calm the situation down. And the 16th Brigade of the Banja Luka Territorial Defence, they had certain problems. And I saw Biljana Plavsic myself. I saw her in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question was: If you did not see them yourself but - from the last part of your answer it is not entirely clear to me who you saw and who you did not see - could you first tell us when you said that Mr. Karadzic arrived on one occasion to calm the situation down, in relation to problems of the 16th Brigade of the Banja Luka Territorial Defence, how did you learn about this visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned about it from my colleagues, officers of the Republika Srpska army. I had regular contact with them. They were my neighbours. We had regular contact. And this was also relayed by the media, because afterwards some officers from that brigade were replaced. Unfortunately, other units were transferred and they were eliminated because there was a rebellion in that brigade. And I personally saw Mrs. Biljana Plavsic in Banja Luka. I was perhaps no more than a metre away from her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us in more detail at what time Mr. Karadzic and Mrs. Plavsic were present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karadzic was there in 1993. It could have been in the month of September, because that brigade or part of that brigade refused to carry out acts of genocide. As the officers acted in a correct manner, they reacted to the problems created by the brigade. There was a risk of a large-scale rebellion. So Karadzic personally appeared. He did not enter the town, but he went to the Trn settlement, which is a municipality on the outskirts of Banja Luka. He, too, was afraid of entering the town because he was afraid that the situation might be chaotic. The situation was calmed down. The officers were replaced. I said some men died as if they had been on the front. And later Mrs. Biljana Plavsic - again, this was in 1993 - I was in front of the Bosna Hotel and she was leaving the hotel with her escort. We passed by each other. That was sometime in the afternoon. I don't know the month though. As for the daily papers, Your Honour, they provided daily reports. The television also provided daily reports about the visits to the corps units, et cetera. That was one of their duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. I was just asking about the time, and you explained a lot more. Two short questions, if possible brief answers. You never saw any member of the Presidency visiting a corps command in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The witness has already said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- expressly that he never saw any of this, so Your Honour is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. -- Mr. Stewart. Did you learn about any visit of a member of the Presidency in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see them personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was whether you learned about any visit of a member of the Presidency in 1992, whether personally or by other sources.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard it from my friends, my fellow citizens of Banja Luka, officers, because I lived in a building where most of the people were officers. Most of them were Serbs. I was the only Bosniak, the only Muslim. We had normal contacts and we had normal exchanges of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us any further details on any such visits as who visited, when this visit took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the visits that were made were not just to the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska but to political institutions, the Crisis Staff, the municipalities. Well, all citizens of Banja Luka, all the Serbs, took a positive view of that. They expected it. It was, you know, the normal visits from the leaders of the Republika Srpska. I myself did not see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Please carefully listen to the question. The question was not whether the Serbs accepted this as normal, but the question was whether you could give us further details on such visits in 1992, and I added to that: Who paid these visits? When took these visits place? I would like you to very much concentrate on the specific questions I put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember now. After all, it was 13 years ago. So I can't really remember when and who made those visits. I did not record it in any of my notebooks, so I really can't confirm the exact dates and who went to see whom. My information at the time was what I'm telling you. I mean, through the media and yeah, of course, you can check it out very easily. You can then check the dates and see exactly who visited where and on what day. But I can't really give you any specific information after 13 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gaynor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I want you to focus exclusively on the year 1992 when you respond. Earlier, a few moments ago, you said, and I quote: "Television also provided daily reports about the visits to the corps units." The first question is: Did you yourself see on television or in other media during 1992 coverage about members of the Presidency of the Republika Srpska, about their visits to the corps command or units at the front?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I remember that it was broadcast on television, and I remember a Lieutenant Pero Colic who later became the Defence Minister of the Republika Srpska. I remember him. I remember General Talic, who was receiving these visits. And from where we stood, it was kind of normal, normal regular obligatory visits. But I really can't recall the exact date. As I said, it was 13 years ago. And I can't give you the date. I'm afraid I might get it wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that ends the -- this portion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, in the -- the same case, the Brdjanin case - and the reference to this is 12905 - counsel asked you, he said: "I wanted to ask you about the relationship between the military and the political wings of government and I want to deal first of all with it at the top level. What was the relationship between those, the politicians at the republic level and the army at Main Staff level? In other words, who was in charge?" That was the question. The first bit of your answer then was: "The Assembly of Republika Srpska or the Assembly of the former Yugoslavia was the top authority, the top political authority." Now, whichever Assembly you're talking about, do we take it that in referring to the Assembly as the top authority, you are referring to the fact that it is the Assembly, the parliament, that passes the laws that the other organs of government must implement and obey and the citizens must be obey?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant. Because it was precisely the Assembly that passed the decision about the setting-up of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska as well as passing the law on the armed forces, and it was implemented by the Defence Ministry and the Main Staff. So the Assembly set the tasks that were then carried out by the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you say "the Assembly set the tasks that were carried out by the army," you don't mean any more, do you, than that they passed the law on the armed forces and then left it to the Defence Ministry and the Main Staff to implement those laws in practical terms? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the army had the same goals as the Assembly. Therefore, the laws passed had been discussed and agreed before, and those common goals were implemented by the armed forces in that sense. Then the police force, et cetera. I mean, the Assembly passed the laws and it was clear who had to implement them and within what period of time, but the goals were common. In this case, apparently the goal justified the means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Selak, if a parliament passes a law that sets up a railway system, you don't -- you wouldn't say the parliament runs the railways, would you? Or would you? Would you or wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Obviously there would have to be an institution putting it into practice. But if the Assembly reaches a decision, they also need to say who is supposed to put it into practice and within what period of time. And it's much the same in all the other countries of the world; the parliament decides about the essential segments of the functioning of the state, and then the other institutions put it into practice. And, of course, then there is a reporting system through various committees, representatives, et cetera, and you have the relevant time limits, and then reports goes back all the way to the Assembly once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, do you have any knowledge of the Assembly of Republika Srpska having executive powers in relation to the operations of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The executive arm of the Assembly is the government; that is to say, first of all, the president of the republic, then the government, followed by all the other institutions, the police force, the armed forces, et cetera. They are the executive bodies. The Assembly appoints the government and the president and -- we know who is accountable to whom and who is in charge of the reporting system on a regular and exceptional basis. And we're talking about daily communications, because we all lived in the same area and we were in constant communication on a daily basis. So the information went from the executive bodies to the government, the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska, and then, of course, to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Witness, Mr. Selak, is the answer that you don't have any knowledge? It's a simple answer: You don't have any knowledge of the Assembly having executive powers in relation to the operation of the armed forces, do you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The Constitution of the Republika Srpska speaks clearly on all that, and it states clearly who is responsible for what. I never had to and, frankly, was not all that interested in every single detail of all that. It is regulated by the Constitution and the legal provisions, the relevant legal provisions governing the behaviour and responsibilities of all the relevant bodies within the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say I'm not proposing to pursue this particular line anymore, but also nor am I proposing to -- with this witness to enter into any debate about whether it is correct to say, as was at line 23, that the executive arm of the Assembly is the government. If we start getting into political theory with this witness and political institutions, I suggest we'll be straying outside what he can usefully help the Trial Chamber with. So unless Your Honours were to feel that I should pursue that, I really don't propose to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I don't think that you should pursue it. You're free to do so if you want to, and the Chamber does not insist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if it -- if it assists the Chamber in the search for truth for me to do so, then I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me say the following, black-and-white questions, the relationship between a government and a parliament, is not completely dealt with if you ask someone whether the parliament would have any executive powers of the army, just referring to your example: If you set up a railway system and if a parliament does so, it's usually not done just by saying there should be a railway system. Very often, whether on the legislative level or later in controlling the policy of the government, sometimes parliament is interested to know whether it's Amsterdam or The Hague that are connected by a line, or Delfzijl and Marum, which are two small villages in the Netherlands. So, therefore, I'm just -- I don't want to have any misunderstanding that by putting some black-and-white questions that not all the grey areas are explored. Whether they should be explored, I leave it entirely up to you. But Chamber at least is aware that there's more -- that there's more than just black and white and that there are different shades of grey in existence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I respectfully agree. And if it were as black and white as that, I could have shortened my three years at Oxford University to about a week and gone home. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if that's sufficient guidance for you on how to proceed, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the witness what he was trying to say. Could he specify that. When he said "the Assembly and the armed forces had the same goals," could he clarify his train of thought.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Serb Democratic Party and the Serb Radical Party within the Republika Srpska had members who were members of the Assembly and the Armed Forces of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had the same goals as the MPs of the Republika Srpska. So they had a common goal, to annex -- or rather, to -- for the Republika Srpska to remain within the structure of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And it can be seen in some documents. It is stated explicitly that their wish and their intention was for the Republika Srpska of Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain a part of Yugoslavia and that it was their goal. And if the Assembly passes a law on the defence, on the setting-up of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska, in that case all these people would be called upon to implement those goals. That's what I meant, Your Honour, when I referred to the common goals of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska and the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska. And I stand by what I've said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this mean -- I'm just looking at your answer here. Does this mean that you consider the armed forces, at least a certain extent, to have been very closely connected to the SDS? Because you're saying that many members of the armed forces were also party members, that they were members of the Serb Democratic Party. Let me specify my question a little bit: What I mean is that one could take a different view of things and say that the armed forces must be politically neutral and that they are simply called upon to implement the guidelines and the directions given to them, so to say, by the government, the National Assembly, or the Defence Ministry. And you seem to indicate that the army was extremely closely connected to certain political choices and that it was at the service of those political choices having been made by others and that they were bent on achieving these goals. Is that what you are trying to say? Is that your evaluation of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is indeed correct that the armed forces were in favour and gave their full support to the policies of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska, fully and entirely. Unfortunately, the crimes committed by the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska and also by paramilitary formations active in that area in that period of time, none of the politicians, none of the members of the Assembly ever called for them to be -- to be brought to justice or held accountable. I mean, I would really like for all this not to have happened and for me not to have to sit here and tell you about it. So what I'm trying to say: The armed forces were fully in agreement with the goals set out by the Serb Democratic and the Serb Radical Party in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of a single case of the Assembly of Republika Srpska giving an order or direction to the armed forces as to what to do or not to do apart from legislation that we can read? So leaving aside legislation, do you know of a single case of the Assembly of Republika Srpska giving an order or direction to the armed forces as to what to do or not do?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I know of one case only. When the Assembly of the Republika Srpska asked the JNA - and I think there is a document from the month of April 1992 - well, they asked the JNA to protect the Serb nation and for them to be given assistance and for the Republika Srpska and the Krajinas -- well, for the army to help them remain within Yugoslavia. And I think that this document must have been submitted to this Court at some point. It is from April 1992. I don't know of any other specific cases about them taking any initiative, in terms of protecting their role and their -- especially not that they were trying to hold anyone accountable for those crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Brdjanin case, you were asked by Ms. Korner, she was talking about General Talic, and she said: "We saw also there, Colonel Selak, General Talic saying words to the effect there was" --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could we have a page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 13.149.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "... words to the effect that there was a Muslim Croat coalition to enslave the Serbia people. From what you knew of him - this is General Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Talic - did he generally believe that when he was saying this on television?" You said: "Yes, he did believe that sincerely because he sincerely wanted for the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to come into being, and he did all within his power to obtain that objective. He believed that all the means were good to achieve that objective so they had excellent cooperation with all political structures and with the SDS in particular, and nobody opposed it because they were pursuing the same common goal and that was the establishment of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He believed that firmly and to the very end." Mr. Selak, when you talk about "they" having excellent cooperation with all political structures and with the SDS in particular, who do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The army, the staff of the 1st Krajina Corps, headed by General Talic. Your Honours, there are regular meetings, briefings with the Crisis Staff, with Mr. Brdjanin at its head. Mr. Brdjanin went to the command. His men went there too. For example, Colonel Vukelic, the assistant commander for morale; Colonel Vukovic Gojko, assistant commander for the organisation of the civilian authorities. They would regularly go to the Crisis Staff, exchange information. And on the basis of that, they took decisions. The Crisis Staff and the corps command took decisions in order to realise the objective of annexes the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Yugoslavia. I'd known General Talic for years, and I was familiar with his beliefs, so I stand by what I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no questions in re-examination. I do have one procedural point, and that is I've been asked to read out the exhibit numbers for the transcript. I'll do that whenever you wish, for the Brdjanin transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. Didn't -- were they not read out yet? And another matter is that no numbers have yet been assigned to the 92 bis transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The transcript of this witness's testimony from the 15th of January, 2003 is P733; the transcript from the 16th of January, 2003 was P733A; the 17th of January, 2003, P733B; the 20th of January, 2003, P733C; the 21st of January, 2003, P733D; the 23rd of January, 2003 was P733E; the 24th of January, 2003 was P733F. And we did not tender the transcripts of this witness's evidence from the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, is that all clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, we'll first have a short break. And it might well be that the Chamber has some additional questions for you after that break. So we'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Hanoteau has one or more questions for you, Mr. Selak. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, a while ago you mentioned the Crisis Staff. I would like to know whether you remember when this Crisis Staff was established and in what way did -- way in which this Crisis Staff function change, in the way the decisions were taken, in what way did this have an effect on life in the local community? How -- what would you say? If you could answer that question.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Crisis Staffs were formed at the end of 1991 and at the beginning of 1992 in the territory covered by the JNA -- or rather, the Republika Srpska army. The Crisis Staffs were formed at the level of Republika Srpska. That was the main Crisis Staff. And there were Crisis Staffs formed in municipalities and in districts. Each municipality had its own Crisis Staff, and that was also the case for the various districts, Bosanska Krajina, Eastern Herzegovina, et cetera, et cetera. Each municipality, as I have said, had its own Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staffs took over all the power, apart from military power. The Crisis Staffs took over civilian power. And I'm referring to the police and to the economy. Everything was organised by the Crisis Staffs. They had all the power, with the exception of military power. As far as the military and the Crisis Staffs are concerned, their relationship was in municipalities, regions, and also in the main Crisis Staff of Republika Srpska. There were political organs in the Crisis Staffs, heads of municipalities, chiefs of police of municipalities, of districts, et cetera. And in the main Crisis Staff there were members from the government, et cetera. They had all the power and they were responsible for all the activities in districts, municipalities, and in Republika Srpska as a whole. There was a daily cooperation between the Crisis Staff and the army, and I know that in the case of Banja Luka and the Crisis Staff of Bosanska Krajina, whose president was Mr. Brdjanin, at meetings of the Crisis Staffs there was the assistant commander for morale and legal affairs, Mr. Vukelic who went there, and the assistant commander for the organisation of civilian authorities in the territory of the corps would also -- he would also attend those meetings. That was Colonel Vukovic Gojko. And there was the corps commander who also attended these meetings when necessary, General Talic. And there was the chief of his staff, Major General Bosko Hlekovic [phoen]. I assume that in other districts things were organised in a similar way because the common objective was to create the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you said that the Crisis Staff had no power over the military, had no authority over the military; however, you say that representatives from the military or their commander attended certain meetings of the Crisis Staff. Why did they attend these meetings in that case? Why did these high-ranking members of the military attend certain meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Well, in order to realise the common objective, Your Honour, because the army was manned with individuals from the territory where the Crisis Staffs were in operation. The army used economic resources for its own purposes. So they tried to coordinate their actions, to implement their goals in municipalities and districts and in the Republika Srpska. So they were trying to coordinate their action and to resolve difficulties encountered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You never attended these meetings of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you as well, Mr. Selak. Could you tell us something about the chains of command of, on the one hand side, the Territorial Defence, TO, and, on the other hand, JNA or VRS at a later stage. Were these chains of command totally separate or was there communication between them? And if so, what type of communication?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honours, the chain of command for the TO went through the Crisis Staffs. Up until 1990, Your Honours, the Territorial Defence in the territory of Yugoslavia was under the republics that had formed them and supplied them and assigned them tasks. The army assisted when it came to equipping them and providing them with trained personnel. After 1990, the Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia took a decision according to which the weapons of TO units should be placed in JNA warehouses. My unit participated in that action in the area of responsibility assigned to me. The idea was to separate the Territorial Defence from the republics because it was believed that Yugoslavia might break up in this way. When the Crisis Staffs were formed - I am now referring to Republika Srpska - they took over the responsibility of equipping and training TO units. Part of those units in certain areas joined JNA units, or rather, the Republika Srpska army, and parts of them, if they didn't become part of the Army of Republika Srpska, remained under the TO in that municipality or in that district. The TO units that were formed at the time, the so-called volunteer units, that General Hadzic decided to form in 1991 - I think that you have that document, Your Honours - well, it was at that time that these volunteer units were established, and they were the responsibility of the Crisis Staffs, not of the army but of the Crisis Staffs. These volunteer units - we also called them paramilitary units because that is what they were - they carried out tasks assigned to them by the Crisis Staffs in municipalities, districts that were assigned to them by the Republika Srpska Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would their activities be coordinated with the JNA/VRS units if the units were not subordinated to the army units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the activities were coordinated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that coordination, who was in charge or who actually coordinated the activities? Was it mainly the Crisis Staff? Was it the command of the regular army units? Was it the command of volunteer units or paramilitary units? Who -- who took the lead in those coordinations?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Crisis Staff took the lead in that coordination because the army units had clearly assigned tasks, and the tasks the Crisis Staff had to deal with were the tasks carried out by the so-called volunteer units, these paramilitary units. So the Crisis Staff was in charge of them. But the army provided officers. There are official documents about this matter in which authorisation is given to manned TO and volunteer units with officers. And authorisation was also given to provide them with weapons, to provide everything that the TO volunteer units needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did this constitute a change in respect of the relations that existed in earlier stages between the JNA and the Territorial Defence? Was this a -- did you consider this to be a change of the structure of relationship between JNA and TO?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. There was a change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to draw your attention again to a certain portion of your evidence you gave in the Brdjanin trial. Part of your answer was read already to you, but I'll extend that a bit. You stated in the Brdjanin trial the following. You said: "The Assembly of Republika Srpska or the Assembly of the former Yugoslavia was the top authority, the top political authority. The Main Staff, or rather, the General Staff of the JNA, or the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska was subordinated to the commander-in-chief. When speaking of Republika Srpska, that is, Mr. Karadzic, he was president of the republic and the commander-in-chief of the Army of Republika Srpska. No other authorities had the powers to command and control the army."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the precise quote is "no political authorities could control the army."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I'll check that in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the version we have says "no other authorities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking now at the relevant page, Mr. Stewart, because of -- to the best of my abilities, I'll try to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it 12.907, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, there might be some confusion. Line 6 says "no other authorities," and line 9 says "no political authorities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, that's quite right. I beg your pardon, Your Honour. It's -- it's got both. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I continue: "And the commander-in-chief of the Army of" -- when you referred to Mr. Karadzic, "He was the president of the republic and the commander-in-chief of the Army of Republika Srpska. No other authorities had the powers to command and control the army. The hierarchy started from a soldier all the way up to the commander-in-chief. That was the chain of responsibility. But apart from that, no political authorities could control the army." Now, you explained to us the first lines of this part of your testimony, where you said that "The Assembly was the top authority, the top political authority." Could you explain to us how you reconcile, if there would be any contradiction at all, the first part of your answer, saying that the Assembly was the top authority, the top political authority, also in view of the explanation you've given, and the last line, where you say that "apart from that" - and you are then talking about the chain of command - "no political authorities could control the army." Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I understand it, Your Honour. When I answered that question, I wanted to say that the Assembly of Republika Srpska took a decision on establishing the Republika Srpska army and then declared a law on the Republika Srpska army. This was their legislative power. The executive organs in the Assembly start with the president of the republic, who is the commander-in-chief, and go right down to the very last private in a unit. Orders are issued from the president, from the commander-in-chief. They're issued to units, and they then go in a reverse order from units to the commander. It's true -- it's quite certain that the president of the republic was duty-bound to inform the Assembly of the results of the tasks carried out by the Army of Republika Srpska. That's what I meant, Your Honour. No institution had the right to issue orders to the army, apart from the fact that I have already mentioned the commander-in-chief, other commanders, and then subordinate units. That's the case in all armies throughout the world because you can't have a dual chain of command in the army. This would result in anarchy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then in an answer just after this, you said: "The political authorities set the objectives and tasks that were to be carried out by the military." In your answer, you were referring to the legislative power, that is, to create, as you said, the Republika -- to establish the Republika Srpska army. Once established, in what way, if at all, was the Assembly still involved in setting objectives and tasks?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. This role was taken over by the commander-in-chief and the Main Staff of Republika Srpska. The Assembly was only informed about the tasks carried out, about the objectives pursued. The Assembly didn't get involved in command and control, but they had to receive information from the army. The president of the republic as the commander-in-chief regularly informed the Assembly of the results obtained by the military and of its operations and the difficulties encountered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were they in a position to comment on the information they had received or to, well, invite the commander-in-chief or the Minister of Defence to change or to adapt their -- their goals or their objectives?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I have no such information on the specific problems that were dealt with at the level of the Assembly. I don't know which issues were dealt with. But this was the usual procedure when it came to the Assembly. The Minister of Defence would provide information on the results obtained and on the activities carried out by the army. He'd be informed -- they'd be informed of the problems encountered. And this was also the case at lower levels, at the level of the municipality. The Municipal Crisis Staffs were in regular contact with the units, and the common problems that arose were dealt with at that level. Problems that could not be dealt with were dealt with at the corps level or at the district level. And if they couldn't be dealt with at that level, then they would try to deal with these problems at a higher level, at the level of the government, et cetera. A minute ago I said that the army used the capacities in the territory, and this was arranged at the level of the Crisis Staff. They agreed on logistical supplies, on medical treatment, et cetera. And if it was impossible to bring -- to man the army from that unit, then this would be done at higher levels. So there was coordination on a daily basis. That is how the system functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, apart from whether it ever happened, could the Assembly in reviewing the report given to it on the objectives and the goals, could they comment on it? Could they disagree and ask the government to do it in a different way or ask the commander-in-chief to adapt their -- his objectives or -- I mean, what -- did they have any controlling function as far as the policy, the objectives, and the goals of the army are concerned?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Assembly is the top legislative body and everybody else is accountable to them, starting from the president of the republic, the government, and it goes for the armed forces as well and their behaviour. So it is only normal in case problems crop up or in case one expects problems, the Assembly must be consulted and must issue its opinion or suggestions or give orders as to how to solve the situation. By way of example, the cooperation between the Republika Srpska and Federal Republic of Yugoslavia run -- run fairly smoothly throughout the war, but it went through the president of the republic, the Crisis Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Staff of the Assembly, and then on their opposite numbers on the other side, in Yugoslavia. And then of course there were certain -- certain problems sometimes, but the Assembly had to check the situation out and they had to be informed on a regular basis about any problems and the tasks of the armed forces and the way in which these tasks are carried out. I do not have specific examples as to what problems were discussed at what Assembly meeting, but that was the way it was done. It was only normal for the armed forces to be accountable to the Assembly. That's the way in which the entire defence system works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gaynor, I asked whether I could be provided with Prosecution Exhibit 1570 in the Brdjanin case. Would it be available?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, we have it here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I have a copy and could you provide a copy to the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's 1572; is that correct, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's 1572 to start with. I also asked for 229, but that's still to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, Exhibit P229 in the Brdjanin case is P192 admitted in this case, and we have copies of that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was not entirely clear to me, whether it was a similar ... Yes, could the witness have a -- be presented with 1572 in Brdjanin. Do you have it in front of you, Mr. Selak?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this document from the 1st Krajina Corps command, it says: "In response to your strictly confidential order number 211541 of 25th of August, 1992, we hereby attach the inventory of weapons and equipment issued to units and TO staffs; in other words, to structures outside the OS" - which stands for "armed forces." Was -- first of all, do you have any knowledge about the equipment issued to structures outside the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, General Hadzic, the Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia already in the beginning issued orders to set up these voluntary units and that they should be issued arms and that people from the army should help them and join them, and the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska did precisely that. They were issuing weapons to those Territorial Defence units which were set up at municipal and regional level, to voluntary units, which were set up in municipalities and in regions, as well as other formations outside the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska. I am informed of that. I informed that I had a problem with General Uzelac, who was the commander of the Banja Luka Corps, who asked me to help create two brigades, at Kozara and Mrakovica and to give them weapons, and I did not issue weapons to them, but the weapons were issued through units who had been withdrawn from Slovenia and Croatia through Bosnia, so they got that quite apart from our logistical base, which was in charge of supplies. So these units were filled and they were given weapons and other equipment by the armed forces, and sometimes even officers went to work with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, just looking at the type of organisations that received these weapons, we see that most of them are identified by "STO." I see many "STOs." Could you explain to us exactly what "STO" stands for. You see: "STO Okucani. STO Kostajnica. STO Glina." Your Honour, it's Territorial Defence staff of the municipality Okucani, Kostajnica, and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sanski Most, Delac [phoen], Laktasi, Celinac. All that is in the Krajina region. So these were -- these Territorial Defence Staffs that were provided with weapons. And then it says: "Other users outside the scope of the JNA." So that's what I mean by those voluntary units and other formations set up by these Crisis Staffs, for their own needs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say "other units outside the JNA" as the last column. In translation, it says: "Other users JNA." Could you perhaps read the original so that we can verify whether the translation is in this respect correct. So could you please read slowly just the words on top of that column so that it can be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: "And other users of the JNA." That's what it says in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Which means other users were in existence; that is to say, the JNA did not need that equipment, and other users were using their equipment. So what is meant basically these -- are these voluntary units that General Hadzic approved and that were set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we find one reference which is different from the others, and that is in relation to Bosanska Krupa, I think. It says: "Brig TO." How should I interpret that, where the others usually say "the staff of the TO."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, this refers to the brigade of the Territorial Defence for Bosanska Krupa. Allow me to clarify this piece of information. At that time -- or rather, by the end of 1991 at a meeting at Banja Luka where I was present and General Hadzic was there, and the decision was made to set up light brigades in municipalities, in regions, the Territorial Defence brigades. And here it refers to the Territorial Defence brigade Kljuc, I think -- no. Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it was -- the equipment was not provided to the Territorial Defence Staff but directly to that brigade. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But the brigade was under the command of the Territorial Defence Staff of that municipality. The other municipalities had not yet set up their brigades, so they could not present them as such. It was up to the staff and then they set up all the other units, battalions, companies, et cetera, depending on how many people they had, what their manning strength was. So that was up to the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And any equipment provided to the staff of the Territorial Defence, could that finally end up in the hands of what you called volunteer units as well or paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Territorial Defence Staff was actually supplying these voluntary and other units with weapons, the other units that they wished to set up for their own purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Even house to house they were distributing weapons to the population. I was an eyewitness in the municipality of Derventa. They were distributing weapons to people at night living in houses which were marked by an "S," Serb, a Serb house. And people would knock on their doors and they would get weapons. And it was done on a broad scale. And even the armed forces participated in that distribution, arming the Serb people, light weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that answer. Could I just have a look at -- Mr. Gaynor, you were so kind to assist to say that Exhibit 229 was a document already in evidence. I -- could I just have a look at it. But perhaps first the document we just reviewed is not in evidence in this case, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There are two possibilities: Either you tender it, or the Chamber will ask it to be -- it relates to the testimony of the witness. You --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. We're happy to have it with a Prosecution exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, then that would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit P741.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I continue, I just want to ... Witness, could you please look at the document in front of you, which is a document where the heading reads "Sanski Most" and the date is the 7th of June, 1992. These are conclusions adopted at a subregional meeting of political representatives of certain municipalities. And as the document says, sent to the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka, the leadership of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo, and the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you any knowledge on who were present at the subregional meeting where these conclusions were adopted?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that this meeting -- that these conclusions refer to a subregional meeting, we're talking about the Bosnian Krajina and the municipalities referred to here, it was the political representatives of the Serb people there, probably from the Serb Democratic Party and other political organisations, because it follows from the text what the reason for this was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: In relation to the Crisis Staff and the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question is whether you have any direct knowledge of persons attending that meeting. I can see from the document that it was a meeting --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we also see in this document that it was sent to the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka, the leadership of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo. Have you ever seen a similar document addressed to, among others, the leadership of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or is it in any other way familiar to you, this way of addressing a document?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had no opportunity to take a look at similar documents. It says: "The Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and then the -- between the word "leadership" and "the republic," it says "Serb republic." And it has been deleted. But I -- I never got to see these documents when I was still in service, in active service. I got them later on. But this is quite clear, this request is clear, because this is a situation that repeated itself later on in the course of the war when, for example, there were documents referring to the Muslims and the Croats having to leave the area. With regard to these institutions, the municipalities, the regions, et cetera -- and some documents even had deadlines, by -- when Muslims and Croats had to leave and unless they did it of their own accord, they would be bussed to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was specifically asking on the way it was addressed to other persons, but I do understand that you could not provide any specific information in relation to that. Since it's already in evidence, we do not have to tender that again. Mr. Selak, I have no further questions to you. But before I give an opportunity to the parties to raise any issue triggered by questions of the Bench first, Judge Hanoteau would have one or more questions for you, additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to clarify one point, sir. Earlier on you referred to units which were equipped and trained by the TOs, and you said they could be described as paramilitary groups or units. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah, I referred to paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In those combat activities that might have taken place, had there been any cases of those paramilitary units fighting alongside the so-called regular army, the armed forces of the republic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. They had a common goal, and for some activities, less complex activities, where the armed forces were not actually needed, they used the services of those voluntary or paramilitary forces and they would dispense with those tasks, arrests, taking people to concentration camps, sometimes even killings or the torching of villages and the destruction of religious sites. And for the most part it was these paramilitary formations or units that were in charge of all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about the regular armed forces? Could they offer some sort of support to those activities engaged in by the paramilitary units? Had there been any cases of the regular armed forces providing support to paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Because there was regular coordination on a daily basis with the TO staff, the Crisis Staff, and the army units in that area. So they agreed amongst themselves who was going to do what in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This coordination or this distribution of tasks, would it have been done on the basis of a meeting within the Crisis Staff or was it just a meeting of Chiefs of Staff or what?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, in the area of the Crisis Staff there was coordination at that level, the Crisis Staff of a municipality or a region. And unless they agreed -- there were no such cases. But in that case, it would have had to go up to the main Crisis Staff or the chief -- the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, but I don't think it has happened ever. It was all done on the basis of regular daily contacts or meetings between army units, the Crisis Staff, or the Territorial Defence Staff, and they would be directly in charge of specific problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any questions triggered by the questions of the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if -- if there would be -- of course, it's -- it's the Prosecution's witness. Of course they tendered the 92 bis statement -- the 92 bis transcripts. But would it not be the logical order first to give an opportunity so that the Defence would have the last --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- opportunity for cross- --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, indeed. I just glanced over and got the impression that they weren't getting to their feet. But I entirely -- I entirely agree with you -- with Your Honour's suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's verify whether the impression is right. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We just have one issue that I want to treat. I'd like just to give Your Honours copies of Prosecution Exhibit 207. I have three copies for Your Honours and a copy for the Defence, and I have a copy for the witness. Now, I'd like ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the Brdjanin number you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, this is admitted in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, admitted in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope you do not mind that not immediately a bell rings when I hear a number. Yes. Further examination by Mr. Gaynor:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'd like you to turn the page and look at paragraph 3. On the English, that's actually on the first page at the bottom. And this document is dated the 28th of July, 1992. It's from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. It's to the SR BH army Main Staff. It's described as a regular combat report. At the bottom appear it is name Colonel Zdravko Djuric [phoen] and this document bears a stamp. Now, Witness, I'd like to direct your attention to that paragraph. Earlier in your testimony today you referred to daily cooperation between the Crisis Staff and the army. You also referred a short moment ago to -- there was regular coordination on a daily basis with the TO Staff, Crisis Staff, and the army units in the area. And His Honour the Presiding Judge drew your attention to some testimony on page 12.907 of the Brdjanin case, lines 16 and 17, where you said, and I quote: "The political authorities set the objectives and tasks that were to be carried out by the military." Now, going back to the document in front of you, this document says: "In the city of Banja Luka and other large towns, there is an increased demand for and organisation of the departure of Croatian and Muslim population. We consider that the municipal and regional authorities should work much harder at this." Now, I'd like to invite your comments on that section of that document.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a regular combat report of the corps command to the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina. This item 3 simply confirms the fact that the Republika Srpska throughout its structure was bent on the departure of both the Croat and the Muslim population from the area that they felt should be the territory of the Republika Srpska. There are several documents confirming this. And certain municipalities even asked for deadlines, as I said. And, for example, in the municipality of Sanski Most, they said unless they left, they would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. organise buses to take these people to Banja Luka so that the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina could deal with it. So this is just reflection of the policy which is being implemented in relation to the planned departure of the Croat and Muslim population from those regions, and that was common practice. By the end of the war, there were about two and a half thousand Bosniaks who stayed in Banja Luka and very few Croats, and before the war there were about 40.000 of them combined.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. Mr. Stewart. Further cross-examination by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel -- Mr. Selak, you were asked at the very beginning of, I think it was, questions by the Trial Chamber, you were asked by His Honour Judge Hanoteau about Crisis Staffs and you gave a rather long and comprehensive answer about Crisis Staffs, including crisis -- "The Crisis Staffs were formed at the end of 1991 and at the beginning of 1992 in the territory covered by the JNA -- or rather, the Republika Srpska army. The Crisis Staffs were formed at the level of Republika Srpska." Now, first of all, Mr. Selak, have you conducted some personal study of the issue of Crisis Staffs in relation to Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honours, as a professional soldier and a logistics base commander, I was preoccupied with this problem because we used the territory of the Bosnian Krajina, in terms of economic resources in order to provide the army units with logistics supplies. So we took advantage of the territory, and I and my bodies wanted to know which institutions we should establish contact with in order to deal with the problems that arose and the institutions concerned were the Crisis Staffs, which had all the power in the areas of their responsibility. So I was interested in the Crisis Staffs. I don't know the names of specific people. I know that in the case of Banja Luka, the president was Brdjanin, et cetera. And the corps bodies also contacted them on a daily basis. Whereas my associates went to municipalities to find logistics supplies, et cetera, for corps units and other units in the area of responsibility covered by the logistics base that I was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, how many Crisis Staffs did you personally have any contact with in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honours, to be quite frank, to provide you with specific information, it was a problem for me to go to those municipalities because I'm a Muslim. My problems developed towards the end of 1991 and were compounded in 1992. To provide you with a specific example: When we were to take over the federal reserves of fuel from Prijedor, I and a group of my experts were to go there. My deputy, Colonel Cendic, a Serb, told me, You won't go there. You shouldn't go there because you'll be risking your life. And from that point in time I avoided going there. My associates went there. But they informed me about how they had dealt with the various issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, what is the answer to my question how many Crisis Staffs did you personally have contact with in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. My men, my associates, would visit all the Crisis Staffs in all the municipalities. They'd go to all the municipalities where the army was present in order to deal with the logistics problems. The area of responsibility of the Banja Luka logistics base was in Bosanska Krajina. But I don't know how often associates went there and I don't know who went there, because there were a lot of them and I wouldn't like to provide you with misleading information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, for the third time of asking, what is the answer to my question: How many Crisis Staffs did you personally have contact with in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I contacted Mr. Brdjanin on two occasions, but I had no contact with Municipal Crisis Staffs. I had contact in Banja Luka with Mr. Brdjanin, but I had no contact with anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the -- where you say, and this was at page 24, line 12, at the end of a long answer: "I assume that in other districts things were organised in a similar way because the common objective was to create the Republika Srpska," that's the basis of your wide assertions of what was happening in relation to Crisis Staffs all over Republika Srpska, isn't it? Common goals.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the common goals of the Crisis Staffs and of the Republika Srpska army. This is quite certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about -- you talked about volunteer units. This was page 28, line 8: "With these volunteer units, we also called them paramilitary units because that is what they were.
