They carried out tasks assigned to them by the Crisis Staffs in municipalities, districts, and that were assigned to them by the Republika Srpska Crisis Staff." Now, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, perhaps before we proceed - because you're referring to pages again - you said at page 24, line 12 there was at the end of a long answer. In my transcript, page 24 of today's hearing reads Mr. Gaynor saying the transcript of this witness's testimony from the 15th of January is P733. So I have some difficulties in identifying --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I -- maybe I just got the wrong reference there, Your Honour. Excuse me one moment. Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. Thank you. No, it's page 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's either my brain or my eyesight, or it could even be both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's hope for the best, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not sure which one I want to lose first, Your Honour. One would be less painful. Thank you, Your Honour. I'll now try and use them both to find where I was a moment ago. Yes, 28, 14, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just to -- well, to remind you, Mr. Selak, it was the sentence at page 28, line 8: "These volunteer units, we also called them paramilitary units because that is what they were. They carried out tasks assigned to them in the municipalities, districts, and that were assigned to them by the Republika Srpska Crisis Staff." Taking first your mention of tasks assigned to them by the Crisis Staffs in municipalities, districts, the position is the same, isn't it, that outside what you've said specifically in relation to Banja Luka, what you say about the carrying-out of tasks assigned by Crisis Staffs in municipalities and districts is based on your assumption in relation to common goals?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. The goals were shared. These were the executive bodies of municipalities, or rather, of the Municipal Crisis Staffs, and they carried out the dirtiest actions. They maltreated people, arrested people, destroyed buildings. But the army participated and assisted in the destruction of buildings. They provided weapons experts. So all the mosques in Banja Luka, 17 of them, were destroyed in Banja Luka, as well as Catholic churches, et cetera. So these paramilitary or volunteer units were involved in the dirtiest actions and the army itself would not have had the time to carry out these actions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also talk, the second limb of that sentence: "These volunteer units carried out tasks that were assigned to them by the Republika Srpska Crisis Staff." Do you have any personal knowledge of any tasks being assigned to paramilitary units by the Republika Srpska Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I don't have such information and I've never seen such documents, but what the Crisis Staff did in the municipalities and in the districts, well, the information was forwarded to the main Crisis Staff, so there was an exchange of information between these Crisis Staffs on a daily basis, and this involved forwarding information and orders. So things followed a regular procedure, and that was the case throughout the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever personally see such information and orders, first of all, passing to the Republika Srpska Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I said that at meetings of the corps command I assisted such -- I attended such a meeting at 7.00, when everyone was present. And in 1992 I was called at 7.30, and in half an hour they dealt with information that I, as a Bosniak, as a Muslim, and as commander of the base was not supposed to hear. So such issues were dealt with before I was present. I wasn't present when those decisions were taken and when such information was passed on. I wasn't present at the time such decisions were taken at any of the meetings because of my nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one follow-up question on that last issue,

utterances.speaker: MR. SELAK
utterances.text: You say -- you told us what was discussed when you were not there yet. How did you learn about that? What happened in your absence?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honours, throughout the war I remained in Banja Luka because I was not allowed to leave Banja Luka. The corps command had issued such an order. And when I retired, my colleagues, my officers in Banja Luka, did not know that I'd been forbidden to leave Banja Luka. And when I stayed in Banja Luka, well, they believed that that was my own decision. And when I had contact with my colleagues, with other officers, we discussed such issues, as well as other political and military issues, and on that occasion they informed me about the events in the region and at a higher level. And it is in this manner that I obtained such information from other officers, colleagues of mine and from other citizens in Banja Luka with whom I had contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has one more question for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there's something else I would like to clarify. I'd like to put the following question to you: When a volunteer or paramilitary unit is engaged - that's what you have called them - you said in response to a question that I put to you that engaging this paramilitary force was the result of a decision taken by the TO Main Staff. What I would like to understand is whether this decision, this order issued by the Main Staff that engaged the paramilitary force, was this decision -- was this order the result of a discussion held at the Crisis Staff? Could you confirm that the Crisis Staff was directly involved in issuing orders for such-and-such a paramilitary unit to participate in an action in a given battlefield?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that Your Honour doesn't like me to get on my feet when Honourable Judges are asking questions, but I would respectfully suggest that if one were more specific about which Crisis Staff, it would avoid any possibility of misunderstanding, before the witness answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to a Crisis Staff of the municipality in which you held your position. I don't want to generalise.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Crisis Staff of the municipality - of the municipality of Banja Luka, if that's the municipality we are referring to - also had the civilian police under them and the volunteer units that it had established. These units were not directly involved in fighting the other side, the Army of the Republic of Croatia, of Bosnia-Herzegovina, et cetera. They were involved in carrying out actions that the police in Banja Luka could not carry out. That involved moving people out, confiscating weapons, destroying buildings, et cetera, et cetera. So these paramilitary forces were equipped by the army, were armed by the army. And, Your Honours, in 1991 the army even provided them with helicopters, military helicopters. This document is one that we have. The army armed them, but they did not get involved in the details in how their tasks were carried out. It's the -- it was the Crisis Staff of a given area that was responsible for such matters, if I have been sufficiently clear. So the army did not command those units. They equipped them. They trained them. In the case of Banja Luka, the training was provided at the Manjaca training ground. That was a military training ground used to train the tank [realtime transcript read in error "task"] corps of the JNA, and later it was a prison, a camp. And this is where paramilitary forces, the Red Berets, et cetera, were trained. And Bogdan Subotic was in charge of this at the time, who was later to become the Minister of Defence in the government of Republika Srpska, and General Talic on the 1st of June, 1991, ordered that these paramilitary forces should be withdrawn from Manjaca because at the time a prisoner camp was being established at the training ground in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like a precise answer to my precise question. In order to engage paramilitary forces, was it necessary to have a decision taken by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the record, page 52, line 11 is tank corps, rather than task corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I ask a question arising out of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever an issue is triggered by Bench questions, you are allowed to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the last answer, Mr. Selak, where Judge Hanoteau said -- he invited a precise answer to the question in order to engage paramilitary forces was it necessary to have a decision taken by the Crisis Staff, and you answered yes. Mr. Selak, I put it to you the position was this: That the paramilitary forces were in many instances a law unto themselves and didn't need and didn't require a decision taken by anybody for their activities. In many instances they just went ahead and just did what they did. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, that's not correct. How could an armed group go into action in the territory of a municipality where there was a police force and where there was an army presence without the authorities being aware of the fact? This is not correct, Your Honour. The municipal authorities were responsible for such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Witness, your -- your answer contains a question, which -- and I'm not here to answer questions. But do you say, then, that there was no activity in Banja Luka -- let's define it to 1992. There was no activity by paramilitaries in Banja Luka in 1992 that was not taken pursuant to an order or decision of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Green Berets [as interpreted] had their headquarters in the Bosna Hotel in Banja Luka. It's a paramilitary organisation. And they were members of the so-called Serbian defence forces in Banja Luka. And they set up barricades and the authorities were aware of this. And in front of the Kozara barracks there was an armoured brigade in those barracks, et cetera. In the course of the day, weapons were sold to the inhabitants over there. So they were active, but none of the members was arrested by the authorities for their manner of conduct. I never heard of any such case. They were in the Bosna Hotel, and I was there for a month as the head of the group for cooperation with the UN. I was then replaced. But next to my office there was also the office of the Red Berets, and their training was provided at the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... make a correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: There was an interpretation error. At page 54, line 2, the transcript reads: "Green Berets."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's -- at least sounds not very logical in view of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think the witness said Red Berets in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you said that the berets had their headquarters in the hotel in Banja Luka, did you refer to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Red Berets, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The same colour discrepancy had struck Mr. Gaynor and me, Your Honour. I was going to say to clarify, we are talking and it's apparent that we are talking about Serb paramilitaries, and that was the purpose of my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Selak, you -- you have referred more than once in the last few minutes to the authorities being aware of these activities. My questions to you are focussed not on whether they were aware of these activities but whether there was a decision or order, which was an answer you gave a few minutes ago. And what I'm putting to you is -- or I'm asking you: Are you saying that - and I'll make the express qualification - are you saying that in 1992 there was no Serb paramilitary activity in Banja Luka that was not pursuant to a decision or order of the Crisis Staff? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I had -- did not have access to the orders issued by the Crisis Staff, but the army did not expel the inhabitants in Banja Luka. They did not make threats. It was the members of these organisations that were involved in such activities. There was the notorious red van which in the course of the day and especially at night went around and they arrested people. Tens of -- scores of people were killed in the vicinity of Vrbas. This was never investigated. And this was done by the paramilitary organisations. Who issued such orders to them if it wasn't the Crisis Staff or someone from the Crisis Staff? Well, I don't know. It was probably not the army. The army did not get involved in such minor operations. The volunteer units were involved in such operations. And they were under the Crisis Staffs in the municipalities. This is true and this can be confirmed by all the inhabitants who lived in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, you don't know yourself whether anybody issued that group with orders, do you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Well, then a state of anarchy prevailed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, please -- please answer my question. I'm not asking you to speculate or theorise. I'm putting it to you you do not yourself know whether anybody issued that group with orders, do you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I wasn't present when the orders were issued or when the groups were established. I wasn't present when they were assigned tasks. But if they were present in a municipality, we know who had the power in that municipality and who could have dealt with such matters, and that was the Crisis Staff. They could have authorised them to carry out certain actions or prevent them from carrying out certain actions. This wasn't done, so one can draw the relevant conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, conclusions in the end do seem to be for the Trial Chamber, so I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions from the Prosecution. Mr. Selak, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for having come the long journey to The Hague. We'd like to thank you for answering the questions of the parties and of the Bench. I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Selak out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that I have contributed to establishing the truth, and I hope that will have assisted in ensuring that everyone will be held accountable for what they did. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibits are P733 to P741.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I hear no objections, they're admitted into evidence. Before we adjourn for the day, because I take it that your next witness is not yet available, or is the next witness available?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: He's not yet available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not yet available. When will the next witness will available?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: He'll be ready tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we adjourn, I'd like to deliver one decision. That is a decision on two sets of contextual exhibits and on the Brcko dossier, and it also contains a directive on the municipality dossiers in more general terms. This is a decision on the admission into evidence of contextual exhibits for Witnesses 73 and 84, as well as of the Brcko dossier. The Chamber will also take this opportunity to issue guidelines for the submission and admission of the remaining dossiers. As for contextual exhibits of Witnesses 73 and 84, the Chamber recalls that it provisionally admitted them on the 19th of April, 2005. The Defence had an opportunity until the 9th of May to raise objections and did not do so. The Chamber wishes first of all to make it clear that, in order to be admitted, all contextual documents must be of real assistance for a better understanding of the testimony of the witness to which they relate as well as for the determination of issues central to the case. The Chamber has reviewed the material submitted by the Prosecution in relation to Witnesses 73 and 84. The Chamber is satisfied that they meet these criteria and therefore admits them into evidence. I will now deal with the Brcko dossier. On the 26th of April, the Prosecution provided the Brcko dossier to the Defence. On the 12th of May, the Defence sent its observations to the Prosecution. On the 15th of May, forwarded them to the Chamber. On the 19th of May, the Chamber provisionally admitted the Brcko dossier. The Defence did not object to the admission of the dossier but made suggestions to improve its usefulness; namely, to add cross-references to already admitted exhibits, to make double-sided copies of the dossier, to provide a hyperlinked CD of the chronology, to translate the chronology into B/C/S, and to include in the dossier a municipality map, a separate index, a municipality dramatis personae and a continually updated running list of witnesses heard and to be heard in relation to each municipality (with date and page references and a list of items admitted into evidence). The Defence also proposed that the chronology be revisable at any time in order to incorporate its suggestions and that a procedure be followed in order to add new Defence items to the dossier. The Chamber considers that the municipality dossier should contain only documents which are of real assistance for the determination of issues central to the case as well as for a better understanding of the evidence already admitted for each municipality. In this regard, the Chamber has reviewed all material provided in relation to Brcko municipality and is satisfied that they meet the above standard. It therefore admits them into evidence. Furthermore, the Chamber invites the Prosecution to assist the Defence as much as possible by implementing the requests made by the Defence in its submissions dated the 12th of May. Perhaps because the Chamber and the Defence have different working methods and archival systems, the features requested by the Defence are not regarded as essential for the Chamber's purposes. The Chamber is content to receive the documentary exhibits with neutral - and I emphasise neutral - index to the contents of each dossier. The additional features requested could be provided separately to the Defence and need not be exhibited, since they are not in themselves evidence. Another reason is that the Chamber does not want to insist on implementation of the Defence's very helpful and sensible suggestions is that we are running out of time. This will become apparent - if it isn't already - in what I next have to say about the schedule for the remaining dossiers. I therefore turn to the future process for the municipality dossiers. As ordered in the April scheduling order, the Prosecution must close its case in chief no later than the 22nd of July, 2005. The admission of dossiers is a process that must be completed well before that date so that the parties and the Chamber have the time to deal with any issues that individual dossiers might give rise to. In the Chamber's mind, it is necessary now to map out the dossier process to fit the trial schedule. It is also necessary to put a ceiling on the amount of evidence that comes in through the dossier process so that the Defence and the Chamber can better foresee and respond to their weekly workloads. The Chamber's ruling on the remainder of the dossier process is as follows: First point: The Prosecution is to stagger its submission of municipality dossiers into seven steps. The next set of municipality dossiers will become due this Friday, the 27th of May. The last set will become due on Friday, the 8th of July. That's a total of seven Fridays, and that means roughly five municipality dossiers each Friday for the next seven weeks. I say "roughly" because 36, not 35 municipalities remain. No municipality dossiers will be admitted after the 8th of July. Second point: The number of documents to be submitted may not exceed 10 documents per dossier and 250 documents in total (including the Brcko dossier). It's for the Prosecution to make what it considers the best selection of documents which, as mentioned above, are of real assistance for the determination of issues central to the case, as well as for a better understanding of the evidence already admitted for each municipality. The Chamber may authorise the Prosecution to exceed the limit of 10 documents per dossier if good cause is shown. As for bulky documents, the Prosecution must tender into evidence only the parts which are strictly relevant for the case. Third point: Each batch of roughly five dossiers will be submitted to the Defence and the Chamber at the same time. A provisional exhibit number will be assigned to each dossier. A provisionally marked dossier will be considered admitted into evidence after seven days have elapsed, unless, in the meantime, any concerns expressed by the Defence or the Chamber are a cause for delays and amendment to the dossier. Fourth point: The Prosecution is reminded, in accordance with my earlier comments, to provide to the Defence with the requested additional features in the dossiers, if time allows. This concludes the Chamber's decision on the contextual exhibits and the municipality dossiers. This concludes our hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- I did have just a couple of minutes of observation about something, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just -- we -- yes, a couple of minutes will go within the limits tapes allow us, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it's this: The way in which this last witness's evidence was dealt with is, in the Defence's submission, very unsatisfactory. The -- he was a 92 bis witness with well over 1.000 pages -- I haven't done an immediate count, but well over 1.000 pages of transcript. When a 92 bis witness comes along for cross-examination, at least for a change, the Defence is supposedly in control of what it's going to cross-examine about. And, Your Honour, with a very heavy programme of witnesses, that is of some importance to the Defence. If we are going to come along faced then with the possibility that the Trial Chamber may then be going to explore any area that is in that 1.000-plus pages of documents, then the burden of preparation on our side becomes inordinately greater. Your Honour, the practical suggestion is this, Your Honour: Is that in the very same way -- and I'm not suggesting we're of equal status, Your Honour. But from a practical point of view, in the very same way that the Trial Chamber frequently insists that the Defence - and certainly in response to 92 bis applications - should indicate the areas in which it wishes to cross-examine. If we are faced with a situation like this, we would request that the Trial Chamber give the parties sufficient notice - and one could discuss what that is, but certainly a matter of several days - sufficient notice of such areas that are proposed to be explored by questioning from the Trial Chamber. Otherwise, Your Honour, it simply becomes impossible for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your suggestion is on the record. We'll consider whether we could follow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, anything you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Nothing. We'll -- we'll discuss the matter with the Defence also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then -- Ms. Loukas, I hope that I do not disappoint you when I say that we adjourn for the day upon your arrival. That's not -- there's no causal relationship between the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I was just wondering about that, Your Honour, but I'm pleased to hear that there's no causal nexus.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can assure Your Honours that there's no causal nexus between my co-counsel choosing this very last moment to arrive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It did not even come into my mind, Mr. Stewart. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00. And, Madam Registrar, we are in Courtroom II again? Yes, Courtroom II.
